High Frontier Computing 1958 to 1982 — Section-by-Section Summary

This is a detailed summary of the document High Frontier Computing 1958 to 1982, a history of numerical modeling and simulation ("computational science") in Texas — chiefly UT Austin and Houston — during the mainframe era. The through-line is that Texas computing grew out of very practical needs (working the land and defending it: oil, aerospace, defense) rather than the science-fiction imagery of space travel and "electronic brains." The narrative traces a handful of real breakthroughs — Simplex, ADI, SOR, subsurface modeling, and orbit determination — from Los Alamos human computers through Santa Monica (RAND/TRW) and Houston (Exxon/Rice) to Austin (UT Computation Center).

The document has four major parts plus a conclusion: Space Age Texas, Modeling The World, Galaxy In The Machine, and Conclusion.

Part 1: Space Age Texas

Space Age Texas (overview)

Sets the frame: Cold War and Space Race pressures, oil-industry demand, academic breakthroughs, and political maneuvering combined to seed world-class computing in Austin and Houston, though it went largely unnoticed at the time. Lyndon Johnson's national influence (National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958, chairing the Space Council) steered federal money to Texas, anchoring the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston. UT Austin benefited too — the 107-inch telescope at McDonald Observatory (1968) and a campus engineering/computing revolution. The underground Computation Center beside the UT Tower (built to house the CDC 6600, with its 400,000 transistors, 100+ miles of wiring, and Freon cooling) faces the LBJ Library — a symbol of the era. Byron Tapley's ~50-year career (orbit mechanics program 1961, department chair 1966–77, later the Center for Space Research) exemplifies the period. The "Los Angeles Model" of aerospace saturated and dispersed talent to Sunbelt schools; UT built links to JPL (the "Texas Mafia" of alumni) and to Exxon in Houston.

The Defense Education Act And NASA

The 1958 National Defense Education Act and National Aeronautics and Space Act together militarized the justification for education funding after Sputnik, creating the modern research-university and federal student-loan systems. UT's engineering programs leapt from mechanical calculators to supercomputing within a decade. Physics doctorates surged (G.I. Bill, defense spending); NSF funded curriculum reform (Physical Science Study Committee under Zacharias; The Feynman Lectures on Physics). The broader zeitgeist of "big science" and centralized, computer-driven problem-solving (Manhattan Project, Los Alamos/Livermore, ICBMs, SAGE, particle accelerators) gave way in the 1970s to inward-looking environmentalism — catalyzed ironically by Apollo 8's 1968 "Earthrise" photo. UT physically isolated its commercial engineering complex from the liberal-arts core to blunt protest.

Big Science And Engineering

Describes the deliberate migration of defense researchers back into universities as a knowledge-transfer policy. Example: Harvard Underwater Sound Lab veterans (Paul Boner) founding UT's Defense Research Laboratory (later Applied Research Laboratory / ARL:UT). Slow communications (mail, phone, travel) made interpersonal transfer central. Introduces RAND and TRW (Ramo-Wooldridge) as the intellectual and industrial engines of the Cold War — RAND providing theory (operations research, game theory, systems analysis) and TRW providing systems engineering for LA-area contractors. Two researchers — George Dantzig at RAND and David Young at TRW — are named as the key figures who carried these currents into Texas, alongside the parallel evolution of floating-point hardware and computerized linear algebra.

George Dantzig

Dantzig's Simplex method for linear programming was a watershed that drove commercial computing and reshaped the oil industry. LP solved the refinery "blending problem," eliminating "quality giveaway" (over-blending expensive high-octane components). Oil companies (Texaco, Humble Oil/Exxon, Shell) became early major mainframe buyers (IBM 701 in 1952, 704 in 1954, rentals >$15,000/month), effectively subsidizing IBM's transition to mass production. This funded UT Austin and Rice computation centers and created the "Texas model" feedback loop (energy profits → university computing → aerospace/semiconductor booms). Covers Dantzig's WWII work in the Army Air Forces Statistical Control Division ("Whiz Kids"), where hand-planning "programs" convinced him a universal mathematical planning method was needed; a 1946 retention offer challenged him to mechanize planning, leading to the 1947 LP formulation. Also covers the broader technocratic shift — Statistical Control veterans (McNamara, Thornton) transforming Ford; the migration of "management by numbers" to Exxon; and the limits/blind spots of pure quantification. Dantzig's work founded Operations Research, Systems Analysis, and Systems Engineering (ICBM program with Ramo-Wooldridge), later powering modern logistics (Amazon, FedEx).

Simplex Linear Programming

Details the 1947 LP formulation and Simplex algorithm, "uniquely machine-ready" and co-evolving with the first stored-program computers. Project SCOOP funded the National Bureau of Standards' SEAC ($400,000); in 1951 SEAC solved the first electronic LP problem (48 equations, 71 variables) in an 18-hour run. The Air Force installed the second UNIVAC I in the Pentagon (1952). Orchard-Hays's "collapsed vector" method squeezed sparse LP matrices into the IBM 701's 2,048-word memory. Explains the meaning of "program" (a schedule) vs. "coding," and Simplex's geometric insight (optimum lies at a vertex of the feasible convex polytope; iterate along edges). Dantzig's brute-force illustration: 70 men/70 jobs by permutation would take "a solar system full of nano-second computers running from the big bang until the universe grows cold." Also notes that early "computers" were rooms of (often women) desk-calculator operators, so the first programmers were often women (Leola Cutler, Ida Rhodes). Dantzig blurred boundaries between modeler, coder, and human computer, personally implementing Simplex at RAND from 1952 with Orchard-Hays (working in octal, pre-Fortran). Sets up the LA "knowledge network" — Western Development Division under Schriever (1954), Ramo-Wooldridge as systems arm, the "concurrency" acquisition concept, PERT.

RAND

RAND (Project RAND 1946 within Douglas Aircraft; independent nonprofit 1948) was the first R&D lab dedicated to modeling and simulation, comparable only to Los Alamos and Bell Labs. It institutionalized systems analysis and game theory (von Neumann, Morgenstern; dynamic programming). A 1954 base-vulnerability study shifted US nuclear doctrine to second-strike deterrence. RAND was an early "hacker lab," building its own JOHNNIAC (1954, 40-bit, von Neumann architecture, first operational core memory ~1954–55, ~5× more reliable than the IBM 701, but no floating-point hardware). JOHNNIAC was a testbed for early AI and timesharing. Covers: Hitch & McKean's The Economics of Defense in the Nuclear Age (1960) and McNamara's Planning-Programming-Budgeting System (1961); RAND's birth of symbolic AI (Newell, Simon, Shaw; linked lists → Information Processing Languages → precursor to Lisp; Logic Theorist, General Problem Solver); Paul Baran's distributed/packet-switching concept ("On Distributed Communications," 1964, "I built a cathedral"); the RAND Tablet/Grafacon (1964); and JOSS (Johnniac Open Shop System, ~1961–62) — an early conversational timesharing system. Notes that much of this work migrated to RAND's spinoff SDC and the SAGE Q-32, and thence to UT Austin (via Forest Baskett).

IBM CPC At RAND

The 1952 "heroic age" — implementing Simplex on the IBM Card-Programmed Electronic Calculator (CPC), a hybrid electromechanical assembly of punched-card machines needing constant human intervention. Traces CPC origins to Northrop Aircraft (1946): engineers merged an IBM 603 multiplier and 405 accounting machine (the "poor man's ENIAC," nicknamed "Betsy"), violating IBM rental agreements; IBM commercialized it (with the 604) in 1949; Rex Rice's general-purpose control panel followed. Traces the deeper ancestry to 1943 Los Alamos (with a long James Gleick quote about Feynman, Metropolis, and IBM punch-card machines). On the CPC, Dantzig and Orchard-Hays reinvented Simplex: the standard tableau was impossible, so they created the Revised Simplex Method (1953) and the Product Form of the Inverse (storing the inverse as products of Eta vectors on cards), exploiting sparsity; Orchard-Hays engineered pseudo-double-precision via BCD column-shift. This solved LPs of ~45 constraints/70 variables (Stigler diet problem), establishing the principle of computational economy — a foundation for HPC. Software lineage evolved to LP/90 on the IBM 7090. Notes UT Austin inherited an IBM CPC from Humble Oil in 1958 via Frederick (Al) Matsen (faculty physically carried it into Welch Hall).

Exxon And Bill Drews

Dantzig's 1960s collaboration with Exxon's Bill Drews carried LP from defense into global industry. Drews studied under Dantzig at Berkeley (1962); the Drews–Rapoport Harvard Business Review paper "Mathematical Approach to Long-Range Planning" (1962) extended LP to multi-decade capital planning. Traces earliest oil-industry LP: Gulf Oil (Cooper, Mellon, Charnes, 1949–52) solving octane giveaway; Symonds's 1955 Linear Programming: The Solution of Refinery Problems; T.E. Baker's later MIMI scheduling system. Covers the Dantzig–Wolfe Decomposition Principle (1959–60), Dantzig's proof of the "Drews Institutionalized Divvy Economy" (1973), shadow-pricing/internal-market simulation, and sparse-matrix computation (Markowitz's 1957 pivot rule; Kalan's "supersparsity" and Ketron's MPS III for IBM 360). Exxon formalized its Mathematics and Systems group (1967), hosting luminaries (Grace Hopper, Bob Bemer, Dimitri Bertsekas). Then pivots to Exxon Production Research at Buffalo Speedway (Houston) — a Bell-Labs-like earth-science center that pioneered 3D seismic imaging, reservoir simulation, and deep-water drilling, driving demand for Cray supercomputers; united with aerospace labs by reliance on the finite-difference method and the "inverse problem" (seismic imaging alongside gravity modeling and weather forecasting). Notes the porous UT/Rice/Buffalo Speedway research triangle (Exxon employed 2,500+ UT alumni).

David Young

Frames the early-1950s simultaneous births of SOR (Young), ADI (Rachford, Douglas, Peaceman in Houston), and Simplex (Dantzig at RAND) — all tied to the IBM CPC or precursors, all establishing linear algebra as the tool for solving physical PDEs and optimization. SOR is an iterative method that "relaxes" a sparse grid system toward a solution using an acceleration factor. These pre-Fortran algorithms motivated capital investment in mainframes and hardware floating-point (IBM 704, 1954; 36-bit word standard). They marked the shift from human-centric, artful, trial-and-error methods (e.g., Southwell's relaxation, which Southwell said could never be mechanized: "Any attempt to mechanize relaxation methods would be a waste of time!") to automated science answering "What do I do next?".

SOR Successive Over-Relaxation

SOR and Simplex ended the human-computer era. Young worked at Aberdeen Proving Ground on the ORDVAC (1,024 40-bit words, no external storage), where iterative methods bypassing direct inversion were essential. Explains FDM: discretizing PDEs onto a grid produces sparse matrices (5-point central difference); direct elimination suffers ruinous "fill-in" (a 100×100 grid → 10,000 variables → 100 million storage locations, impossible on early machines). SOR sweeps the grid using only non-zero coefficients, keeping memory proportional to variables. The "over-relaxation" factor omega extrapolates the correction; Young proved that for matrices with "Property A" the optimal omega gives an order-of-magnitude speedup. Kahan (1958) proved omega must be strictly between 0 and 2. SOR crossed into optimization (Projected SOR for LP inequalities) and machine learning (training Support Vector Machines on up to 10 million points). At UT, Young founded the Computation Center and Center for Numerical Analysis, and his group produced ITPACK (Fortran SOR subroutines).

Ramo-Wooldridge And TRW

The mid-50s ICBM program (Atlas, Titan, Thor) demanded fast PDE solving for atmospheric reentry (plasma sheath, heat/fluid flow). Ramo and Wooldridge pioneered systems engineering emphasizing digital simulation. Young was recruited (1955) to head the Numerical Application Section in the Guided Missile Research Division. Because Soviet rockets were far more powerful (R-7 ~1,000,000 lb thrust vs. Atlas ~150,000 lb), the US compensated with extreme structural optimization (Ramo's "ten-to-one" structure-to-fuel ratio; the Atlas so light it would collapse unfueled). This required solving huge sparse matrices — Young's SOR was the critical tool. RAND and TRW functioned as a symbiotic relay (RAND theory, TRW hardware); both looked more like universities than aerospace firms; Schriever rejected traditional airframe makers for lacking scientific competence. TRW's Inglewood HQ was the "Schoolhouse." The Air Force "hardware ban" (conflict-of-interest exclusion) forced TRW to specialize in simulation as its product; Space Technology Laboratories spun off into the nonprofit Aerospace Corporation (1960, 1,700+ employees). SOR-driven reentry simulation let engineers cut the Atlas from 460,000 to 240,000 lb, saving ~a year. SOR-based Fortran programs became the repository of US aerospace knowledge; Young carried the legacy to UT (1958).

UNIVAC 1103A Scientific And Floating-Point

TRW's UNIVAC 1103 used fragile Williams-tube (CRT) memory (1,024 words) so temperamental that even car spark-plug noise could flip bits, ruining long SOR runs. The 1103A (April 1957) introduced magnetic-core memory (non-volatile, reliable, up to 12,288 words) and optional hardware floating-point — a historical turning point from slow software emulation (TRW's SNAP interpreter, IBM's Speedcoding) to single-instruction hardware ops (10–50× speedup). The 1103A used a 36-bit format (1 sign, 8 exponent, 27 fraction). This launches an extended history of floating-point:

  • Zuse's European lead: the Z3 (1941, first binary floating-point hardware) and Z4 (1945, 32-bit), built for aircraft flutter/stress analysis at Henschel, anticipating rounding protocols and special values (infinity/NaN); Z4 later at ETH Zurich. American doctrine (championed by certain theorists) favored fixed-point, ceding the vanguard to Zuse.
  • Other machines: Bell Model V (1946); Manchester machines (no FP); Ferranti Mercury (1957, no hardware division); Soviet BESM-1 (1952) and BESM-6 (1967).
  • The IBM 704 (1954) broke the deadlock as the first commercial hardware floating-point machine; Fortran (Backus) and the FP hardware (Backus, Amdahl) were co-developed; 704 descended from SAGE/Whirlwind; CAR/CDR named for its address/decrement fields; 36-bit standard carried through 709/7090/7094 (Mercury/Gemini computed on these).
  • The "zoo" (Kahan): no standard before IEEE 754 (1985); wildly varying bases, word lengths, exponent schemes; bizarre coping tricks (x = x + x - x).
  • IBM System/360 (1964): hexadecimal floating-point caused "wobbling precision" (21–24 bits), frustrating numerical analysts, requiring a 1968 guard-digit retrofit, and opening the market to CDC/Cray's superior 60-bit machines.
  • Portability nightmares (36-bit vs 32-bit vs 60-bit divergence) and hand-tuned math libraries per architecture; the "zoo" served as an evolutionary lab producing IEEE 754. Ends by returning to Young implementing SOR on the 1103/1103A (1955–58), both designed by ERA (later CDC) with early Seymour Cray design credit — foreshadowing UT's later CDC/Cray ties and the scaling from 36-bit → 48-bit CDC 1604 (1960) → 60-bit CDC 6600 (1966).

UT Austin And Numerical Analysis

Young moved to UT in 1958 to found the Computation Center (initially just Young, Robert Gregory, a secretary, and an IBM 650). Within 18 months he secured a $400,000 NSF grant for a CDC 1604, and in 1966 the first $1,000,000 NSF grant toward a CDC 6600 (Gregory: "David Young did it"; UT was the first university with a 6600, ahead of Berkeley, Stanford, MIT, Harvard). Covers the maturation of numerical linear algebra: the realization that electronic speed ≠ numerical truth (rounding-error accumulation); Wilkinson's backward error analysis (rescuing Gaussian elimination via partial pivoting; the Hilbert matrix; crediting Givens 1954); matrix factorizations (LU — Banachiewicz 1938; QR for least-squares); and the SVD (Golub & Kahan, 1965) as a "Swiss Army knife" for ill-conditioned/rectangular matrices. Notes high-profile 1960s successes: NASA orbit/launch decisions on IBM 7090; gravity-assist trajectory proofs (UCLA); and computerized weather forecasting (ENIAC 1950; Hurricane Betsy 1965), where the CDC 6600's 60-bit word gave "double precision at single-precision speed."

UT Computation Center

Frames UT's two-decade evolution (1958–~1979) via two intertwined threads: Al Matsen (chemistry, Welch Hall, IBM hardware, oil-industry pragmatism) and David Young (math, Benedict Hall, CDC hardware, aerospace systems thinking). The IBM/CDC contrast mirrors the oil-vs-aerospace industry contrast (Exxon = IBM; TRW = UNIVAC; CDC = UNIVAC spinoff). Both men are described as founders/first directors; the 1966 underground 6600 sat midway between Welch (north) and Benedict (south), symbolizing computing outgrowing individual departments.

IBM CPC At UT

Chemistry's 1955 IBM 650 (first real computer on campus, used for Quantum Chemistry Integrals and Tables; Matsen shared it, leading a UT president to complain about a "computer center" that didn't officially exist). In 1958 Humble Oil donated an IBM CPC (Matsen was a 35+ year Exxon consultant; the "What possible use could you be to Exxon?" anecdote); faculty physically carried it into Welch. The CPC (a backward step from the 650) is described in detail as the machine Dantzig used for Simplex in 1952. Then repeats the Young 1958 founding story.

CDC 6600

UT's aggressive pursuit of top floating-point hardware: the $6M CDC 6600 (summer 1966), fastest computer in the world (3× the IBM 7030 Stretch), putting UT in the class of Los Alamos/Livermore/CERN. Architecture (Cray & Thornton, 1964): 60-bit CPU freed for arithmetic by 10 Peripheral Processors (based on the 12-bit 160-A, implemented via "barrel and slot"); 10 parallel functional units, instruction stack, scoreboard, ~3 MFLOPS. UT wrote local system software (UT-2D) linking the 6600 (batch) with a cheaper serial CDC 6400 (interactive timesharing). Parallel/multiprocessing was "in the UTCC's genes," making it more like a national lab than a typical university. Physical detail: underground building (Freon cooling, 400,000 transistors, 100+ miles of wiring, "cordwood" modules, no wire longer than 8 feet, plus-sign shape). Young stepped down as director in 1970 to found the Center for Numerical Analysis (ITPACK). The 6600 began a CDC → Cyber → Cray procurement lineage; the two IBM Welch machines were the last of their kind for science/engineering. Details the 60-bit word's rationale (national-lab shockwave simulations with 10^12 variations; 11-bit exponent, 48-bit fraction ≈ 14 decimal digits; Indefinite/Infinity patterns anticipating NaN; ones'-complement arithmetic with ±0). Also covers CDC idiosyncrasies: no byte addressability, 6-bit characters (ten per word), and UT's adoption of the "63 character set" (also popular in the Netherlands) — a deliberate act of technical independence that seeded an unbroken UT supercomputing lineage (later CHPC → TACC).

The Dual Dinosaur UT-2D

The CDC 6400 (serial CPU) paired with the 6600. CDC's SCOPE OS was too restrictive; UT adopted MACE (from the Chippewa OS), then built UT-2D in-house (COMPASS assembly) — a pair of autonomous, communicating operating systems with innovative cost-based preemptive-resume scheduling that prioritized cheap student jobs. UT-2D lasted into the mid-80s (billing functions into the 90s on the Cyber). The early-70s TAURUS timesharing system (Texas Anthropocentric Ubiquitous Responsive User System) extended interactive access to remote teletypes and graphics terminals. The 6600's open academic setting made it more accessible than oversubscribed national-lab machines, cultivating a local technical/software culture from 1966.

Southwest Network And ARPANET

The 1969 NSF-funded Southwest Region Educational Computer Network (11 colleges + 3 secondary schools by 1972) centered on UTCC; only UT, Rice, and Trinity had sizable facilities. Clarifies that UT Austin was not one of the original four 1969 ARPANET nodes (those were UCLA, SRI, UC Santa Barbara, and the University of Utah, not Texas). UT's first IMP arrived in 1977 (first Texas node), listed in the 1978 ARPANET Directory (Linguistics Research Center and Computation Center); later assigned the Class A network 39.0.0.0 (Balcones Research Center). Describes campus RJE life (punch-card decks at Pearce Hall, Taylor Hall) and the 6600's real reliability (running months without failure; Pi to 500,000 digits over a 60-hour Thanksgiving weekend).

Part 2: Modeling The World

Opens with the 1960s changes at the engineering complex (WRW, 1960; Department of Aerospace Engineering and Engineering Mechanics, 1968), and Tinsley Oden (finite element method) and Byron Tapley (orbital mechanics/geodesy). In the 1970s, modeling grew from point-solutions to whole-field FDM/FEM simulations and satellite geodesy (Earth's geoid, plate tectonics/mantle convection). Oden argued computational science is a "Third Pillar of Science" alongside experiment and theory. The unifying theme: Texas's land/resources/geology extended outward to orbit and beyond via computing, satellites, laser ranging, and communications. Pioneers (Tapley, Schutz, Duncombe, Wheeler) linked subsurface to satellites (gravity field ↔ orbits ↔ geology/sea-surface/interior). The Navy's Transit satellite system (first launch 13 April 1960) revealed the Earth's asymmetrical shape and inadequate gravity models — establishing the satellite as a "test particle" probing Earth's gravity.

TRANET And Ray Duncombe

Roots trace to Sputnik (4 October 1957): Ray Duncombe and Paul Herget (US Naval Observatory) computed Sputnik's orbit around the clock. Astronomy/navigation/maritime ties are emphasized (Duncombe as a link between McDonald Observatory and the Naval Observatory). Minitrack (the first US satellite tracking network, radio interferometry along the 75th meridian) had to be frantically converted from 108 MHz to Sputnik's 20/40 MHz in ~two weeks (jury-rigged antennas at Lima, Peru). Duncombe did a graphical hand solution of the orbit; the IBM 704 at the Vanguard Computing Center ran 154 hours (~6 billion calculations) to produce a definitive ephemeris. Includes a James Gleick anecdote about Feynman out-computing a JPL IBM 704 to correctly predict that Explorer II (1958) failed to reach orbit. Then covers the shift to Doppler tracking (TRANET), operated concurrently with Minitrack; UT ran two TRANET stations (Austin and McMurdo Sound, Antarctica). Emphasizes the maritime/navigation/geodesy blend and the eventual synthesis (via CSR and ARL) of TRANET Doppler + McDonald SLR into the ITRF/ICRF/IERS frameworks. Duncombe joined UT in 1975 (Aerospace Engineering, CSR), took students on field trips to McDonald. Detailed account of McMurdo Station 019 (tracking from 5 Feb 1965; NMSU's PSL then ARL:UT from Oct 1968 for a quarter-century; staffed by one grad + one undergrad UT electrical-engineering student; −50°C conditions; automated in 1971; HF radio → New Zealand → AUTODIN; ionospheric propagation studies enabling dual-frequency 150/400 MHz correction; contributing to WGS 84 and GPS foundations).

McDonald Observatory And West Texas

Laser ranging's core role in space geodesy. Apollo-era lunar retroreflectors enabled centimeter-level ranging (vs. 0.7-mile radar and 180-meter early laser). Velocity aberration favored arrays of small retroreflector cubes; the faint lunar return required a large telescope — a key motivation for NASA funding the 107-inch telescope (first successful lunar returns 19 August 1969; world's only routine lunar-ranging facility for 15+ years). Satellite laser ranging (SLR) developed in parallel: GEOS-3, LAGEOS (1976, first to measure tectonic plate motion, polar motion, Earth's mass, seasonal time-variable gravity), SeaSat (1978, ocean-surface topography). Late-70s Transportable Laser Ranging System → McDonald Laser Ranging Station. ARL built refraction-correction packages and the FICA data format (precursor to RINEX). Extensive geology: McDonald sits on stable ancient craton bedrock (Davis Mountains / Trans-Pecos Magmatic Province, 39–35 Ma ash-flow tuffs and rhyolites; dense trachyte anchoring the 160-ton telescope), contrasted with expandable subsurface reservoirs; fractured volcanic rock stores "rock moisture" that can mimic tectonic gravity signals and recharges springs (San Solomon Springs, Balmorhea); bounded by active faults (Rio Grande Rift, Texas Lineament; 1931 Valentine earthquake). SLR/LLR data yielded Earth Orientation Parameters, North American Plate drift, sea-level/altimetry support (TOPEX/Poseidon, Jason), and even biospheric signals (seasonal tree-sap moment-of-inertia changes; Moon receding 3.8 cm/yr).

Satellites To Subsurface

The reciprocal relationship: a known ground position resolves an unknown orbit, and a known orbit resolves an unknown ground position. Minimizing orbital error shifted focus from navigation to geodesy (satellite as gravitational test particle). This required isolating satellites from non-gravitational forces → "cannonball" satellites with tiny area-to-mass ratios (Starlette, 1975, 14 cm, depleted-uranium core; LAGEOS, dense aluminum/brass). SLR gave absolute distance to the satellite's center of mass. At UT, UTOPIA on the CDC 6600 performed precision orbit determination on these satellites, inverting the data to map Earth's subsurface density — the Earth as a "CAT/MRI scanner." Future: laser-cooled cesium-atom interferometry a million times more sensitive, "rendering the Earth's surface transparent." Gravity modeling emerged as a computational grand challenge alongside subsurface and weather modeling, strengthening UT–Rice–Exxon ties (Mary Wheeler bridging them).

Mary Wheeler

Wheeler first encountered subsurface techniques in Young's UT numerical-analysis course on the CDC 1604. Dynamic PDEs model transient fluid flow/transport in porous media; ADI (Douglas, Rachford, Peaceman at Humble Oil) broke them into 1D steps. Her 1963 UT master's thesis analyzed ADI; at Rice her advisors were Rachford and Douglas (whom she called "the fathers of the field"). She became the first tenured female associate/full professor in engineering at Rice, championed rigorous finite element methods, and later directed UT's Center for Subsurface Modeling (redirecting the tools to groundwater remediation, CO₂ storage, geothermal). Her key theoretical contribution: proving industry's cell-centered finite-difference schemes were simplified approximations of mixed finite element methods (letting industry keep existing code with rigorous justification), and the "elliptic projection" decoupling spatial and temporal error in dynamic simulations (her 1971 dissertation).

ADI And IBM CPC At Exxon Precursor Humble Oil

Connects UT/Exxon/Rice/Houston. Exxon acquired its CPC in 1952 and used it heavily to create ADI (Alternating Direction Implicit, 1954) — decomposing multidimensional PDEs into sequences of 1D problems (modern ADMM is essentially ADI). Detailed CPC description (plugboard programming, ~5 FLOPS, ~56 words of "ice box" counter-wheel memory). Parallel card-manipulation tricks at RAND (Orchard-Hays flipping card decks to transpose) and Houston (card sorter to transpose row/column sweeps), both descending from Feynman's colored-deck human-computer pipelines at Los Alamos (1943). Humble Oil's hardware progression: CPC → Bendix G-15 (1955, 864 words, ~10 FLOPS) → IBM 704 (~1956, core memory, ~10,000 FLOPS) — freeing the CPC for transfer to Matsen at UT (1958), roughly when Young got SOR onto the 1103A.

Early History Of Reservoir Simulation

Pre-digital physical analog models (1930s–40s): water-coning models (1933), wedge-shaped radial models, electrolytic models (East Texas Field), resistor-capacitor networks (voltage=pressure, current=flow), and heat-flow analogs. Their limits (cost, scaling, inability to model nonlinear multi-phase flow) drove Rachford, Peaceman, and Douglas to digital FDM; ADI (1954) bypassed the memory/stability bottlenecks of fully-implicit and explicit schemes. FDM struggled with complex geology ("staircase" boundaries); FEM (weak formulation, unstructured meshes) became standard for solid mechanics but early continuous FEM failed for fluid flow (no local mass conservation) — setting up Wheeler's contributions.

ADI And SOR

Compares the two algorithms and their cultures. SOR came from academia (Young's 1950 Harvard dissertation; nurtured at universities and Oak Ridge; "elegant, pure" linear algebra). ADI was a "gritty algorithmic hack" born of commercial urgency (Dec 1953, Peaceman/Rachford/Douglas). Both fought tiny memory. ADI aligned with IBM (oil, industrial), SOR with UNIVAC/CDC (aerospace, national labs). Deep dive on tridiagonality: ADI splits 2D problems into cheap tridiagonal 1D systems (linear cost); SOR grinds point-by-point but, as Line SOR (SLOR), can exploit tridiagonality too. SOR was memory-frugal (in-place) but omega-tuning was a "dark art"; ADI was more robust (sequence of acceleration parameters) but a memory hog. The methods eventually converged (SLOR reusing ADI's tridiagonal machinery); SOR led to multigrid/preconditioned solvers, ADI to operator-splitting/fractional-step methods still used in climate/CFD.

Subsurface Modeling

Early-70s FEM became a robust competitor to FDM; Rice's 1970 Department of Mathematical Sciences was a catalyst. Wheeler's 1973 "Pipeline in Permafrost" work (Trans-Alaska Pipeline) modeled the moving freeze/thaw boundary (her husband was an Exxon pipeline engineer). She proved cell-centered FDM ≈ mixed FEM, introduced the elliptic projection, developed flux-extraction techniques, and (late 70s) interior-penalty methods for fractured/layered rock. Describes 1970s hardware constraints (hand-coded punch cards, IBM 360, scarce RAM, secondary-storage swapping, superconvergence to extract accuracy from coarse grids). Traces the UT (CDC) vs. Exxon (IBM) hardware parallel, bookended by a shared IBM era (50s) and a shared Cray era (80s): UT moved to the ERA/CDC tradition early (via Young), Exxon followed in the 80s. Both adopted Cray vector supercomputers in the 80s (Exxon for bigger 3D reservoir models; UT for seismic imaging that helped find the Atlantis and Thunder Horse fields). Wheeler's later work: geologic carbon storage (supercritical CO₂ in deep saline aquifers; brine as storage/reactor; dissolution → density increase → mineralization), and a hybrid enriched-continuous method conserving mass with low memory; plus data assimilation combining well-bore and satellite-gravity data.

Bob Schutz

Schutz studied under Tapley (orbital mechanics program, 1961) and became an expert user of UT's 60-bit systems (6600 → Cyber → Cray, ~20 years). Attended NASA's Williamstown workshops (the 1967 session defining the need for a gravity mission; the 1969 report The Terrestrial Environment: Solid Earth and Ocean Physics), anticipating GRACE/GOCE. The 1969 report set goals (geoid to 10 cm, geoid time-variation to 5 cm, crustal motion to 10 cm) and recommended drag-free low-altitude satellites and satellite-to-satellite tracking (the "Geopause" relay concept at 30,000 km; the "Gravsat" low-low pair at ~200 km). Early high-low tracking used Apollo lunar orbiters (mapping mascons) and geosynchronous relays (Apollo-Soyuz, GEOS). UT built UTOPIA (University of Texas Orbit Processor) in 1974. The Navy's Triad mission (1972) validated drag-free flight via the DISCOS system (Lange's 1964 concept; a gold-platinum proof mass floating in a cavity, cold-gas thrusters chasing it; tri-body booms and symmetric donut fuel tanks to null self-gravity), extending Transit ephemeris predictions to a week+. Schutz/Tapley improved Transit orbit uploads with statistical filtering (adaptive state noise, dynamic model compensation), driving the shift from Doppler to SLR. This culminated in the Center for Space Research (1981, Tapley founding director). Long section on the Transit system's origins: Guier and Weiffenbach's Doppler insight (1957), McClure's inversion (orbit → position), the Polaris submarine need, and how gravity-model quality initially dominated navigation error until a crossover made orbit-upload quality dominant — which is where UT (Tapley, Schutz, CDC 6600 numerical integration of full nonlinear equations, and UTOPIA in 1974) entered the story.

Geodesy And Spherical Harmonics

Geodesy models Earth's non-uniform gravity. Early Transit orbit errors reached ~2 km/day; the 0.1-nautical-mile requirement demanded better gravity models. Explains Laplace's equation, harmonic functions, and spherical-harmonic expansion (zonal/latitude, sectorial/longitude "orange slices," tesseral/checkerboard patterns). Draws an analogy to FEM (both decompose complex reality into simpler parts — local mesh vs. global basis functions; pixels vs. compression; musical fundamental + overtones). Challenges: needing dense, globally-distributed data; non-zonal (longitude-dependent) harmonics requiring per-revolution data; TRANET's all-weather Doppler solving this (~100 Doppler sets/satellite/day); needing multiple orbital inclinations; atmospheric noise capping high-order (degree >100) resolution. Slow convergence discovered via orbital resonance (Transit 5BN-2's 130 m, 60-hour oscillation from 13th-order harmonics; 65- and 40-hour beats from 13th/14th order); aliasing from truncating too early. UT was "uniquely prepared" by its 60-bit machine.

CDC 6600 And Cyber

Spherical-harmonic computation is expensive/unstable (recursive differentiation, thousands of correlated coefficients, ill-conditioned normal matrices; one iteration could take 50 hours). Resonance exploited to isolate high-order coefficients cheaply. Software lineage: Celest (batch least-squares) → Prefer (sequential Kalman filter, 120-second mini-batches, dropping out-of-view parameters). Detailed history of the NORC (IBM-built for the Navy Bureau of Ordnance, $1 profit; Eckert at Columbia's Watson Lab; demonstrated 1954; Dahlgren 1955; decimal 14-digit words; ~15,000 ops/sec; used by Patricia Smith's Orki for Transit orbits and Paul Herget for Earth's orbit — who named an asteroid "The NORC"). A "historic computing marathon": simultaneously solving 70 geopotential coefficients (degree/order 8) against 1,662 tracking datasets took ~50 hours on an IBM 7094 in 72-bit double precision with out-of-core block-partitioning on tape (Anderle's team at the Naval Weapons Laboratory, validating TRANET geodesy to 20 m). Software lineage: Orki (NORC) → Astro (IBM 7030 Stretch) → Celest (IBM 360, 1964, Fortran). Model growth: WGS-72 (~500 terms) → modern degree/order 70 (7,000+ terms, ~2 hours on a Cray). Schutz's numerical innovations: three-term recursion (avoiding differentiation), a normalized Pines formulation avoiding polar singularities, and vector-optimized recursion for the Cray. UTCC hardware upgrades: 6600 → Cyber 170/750 and 175 (some at Balcones Research Center) → Cray X-MP (1985, first Cray at a Texas university), enabling gravity models to degree/order 180 (even 300 for low orders). UTOPIA (1974) merged numerical integration with batch least-squares differential correction (Beacon Explorer, GEOS).

McDonald Laser Ranging, Harlan Smith, And Pete Shelus

1970s multi-instrument gravity modeling (SLR + radar altimetry) yielded the first global high-resolution geoid maps, moving beyond spherical approximations. Optical tracking (Baker-Nunn cameras, SAO, ~10–30 m, best global coverage — most valuable for early GEM-9); Doppler (TRANET, 3–7 m; APL models APL 1.0, APL 3.5); merged in Goddard Earth Models (GEM-9, GEM-10). Radar altimetry mapped the geoid over oceans (seamounts, trenches, ridges). SLR (since 1964) evolved from meters to millimeters (eventually requiring General Relativity corrections); Schutz/Tapley gave the first laser-ranging determination of polar motion and validated plate tectonics. Laser's optical advantage: no water-vapor "wet delay" (millimeter vs. tens of cm), enabling UTOPIA's stable modeling; by 1980, 0.2 ns pulses gave 7–15 cm accuracy. LAGEOS (May 1976, 60 cm, ~410 kg, 426 retroreflectors, ~5,900 km orbit for 8 million years) stabilized the terrestrial frame and low-degree harmonics; decorrelated higher harmonics when combined with lower Starlette; enabled geocenter-motion monitoring.

  • Harlan Smith: came to UT in 1963 (Astronomy chair 15 years, McDonald director 26 years); Quaker, peace advocate, science-communicator (The Story of the Universe, StarDate), L5 Society, lunar-base advocate; secured NASA/NSF/UT funding for the 107-inch; served on the committee that helped launch Hubble and proposed the Great Observatories.
  • Hubble/McDonald astrometry parallel to geodesy: McDonald's Texas Minor Planet Program (Hemenway and Raynor Duncombe, 1978; 1,000+ plates; "crossing-point method") provided precise moving targets to calibrate Hubble's fine guidance sensors, linking the Hipparcos/optical system to a dynamical frame.
  • Pete Shelus: hired 1970 to analyze noisy lunar-laser photon returns (Korad ruby laser on the 107-inch); led the transition to the automated dual-purpose McDonald Laser Ranging Station (0.76 m telescope on Mount Fowlkes); four-stage photon filtering; bridged laser ranging and geodesy communities (IERS director of the LLR coordinating center, ITRF/ICRF contributions, Earth Rotation by Lunar Distances campaign, continuing Duncombe's legacy). Explains ITRF (Earth-fixed, realized via ground network) and ICRF (space-fixed, VLBI/quasars, plus LLR dynamical frame); SLR uniquely defines the geocenter and Earth's mass/gravitational constant.

UTOPIA

Data flowed from McDonald to Austin, processed by Schutz's CDC 6600/Cyber code — embodied in UTOPIA (University of Texas Orbit Processor). Two generations: EARTHOD (Fortran IV on the 6600, a simulation program generating measurements for up to 12 stations, used to test adaptive/filtering procedures; revealed that localized short-arc Cartesian filters were structurally inadequate) → UTOPIA (operational, unlimited global networks, batch least-squares + extended sequential filters including the square-root information filter; multi-week arcs; thousands of parameters). UTOPIA validated NASA's Geodyn and Germany's EPOS independently (e.g., LAGEOS frame-dragging tests over 11 years). Extensive technical detail: over-determined estimation; square-root information filter/smoother and UD covariance factorization (doubling effective precision, avoiding filter divergence); CDC memory limits (18-bit addressing → 262,144-word ceiling; extended core storage for block swapping); the state-transition-matrix approach (Taylor-series linearization about a reference trajectory, mapping observations back to a single epoch); operating on information arrays rather than covariance matrices; Givens/Householder orthogonal transformations; and Schutz's fully-normalized rectangular spherical-harmonic formulation (1973 base + normalization) removing polar singularities and overflow/underflow — unlocking scalability (LAGEOS integrations extended 3 → 24 hours; SeaSat/TOPEX; eventually 70×70 and 180×180). Also covers consider-covariance analysis (accounting for un-estimated parameter uncertainties), the Starlette 74-day polar-motion perturbation study, JGM-3 and CSR 3.0 ocean-tide models (2–3 cm radial accuracy), the Ajisai 3-day sub-arc control-point estimation (3–4 cm), and LLR linking ITRF to ICRF (lunar tidal acceleration, 3.8 cm/yr recession). Ends by contrasting UTOPIA (remote, productionized, operational) with the earlier all-encompassing 6600 era where numerical code (EARTHOD) coexisted with student projects — setting up Part 3.

Part 3: Galaxy In The Machine

Returns to the late-60s/early-70s CDC 6600 era as a special shared community. Punch-card computing forced everyone (aerospace researchers to undergraduates) into the same terminal rooms, an "intellectual commons." Describes punch-card logistics (a card per line, keypunch operators, "gofers" running decks), the extreme case of the CPC (human as manual control unit re-feeding decks for loops), and long batch turnaround where a single syntax error meant restarting. A second unifying force: computer games. CDC's own checkout engineers used the 6600's CRT consoles for diagnostic games (Space Wars — a fast version of MIT's 1962 PDP-1 Spacewar; Lunar Lander; Baseball, cited in Magnavox patent suits) to stress-test machines. At UT this blossomed into a multi-generational family of Star Trek–inspired space simulations from the late-60s CDC 6600 to the early-80s DEC-10 — the story that ties the section together.

National Science Foundation

NSF funded the 6600 (the $1M 1966 grant) and later helped introduce the DEC-10. Two initiatives broke the "Anastasio cycle" (powerful mainframes but no good educational software): Project C-BE (Computer-Based Education, launched 1972; Lagowski and Allan; 75 professors, 4,000+ students, 44 projects, 27 courses; wired Kodak slide projectors to terminals; the SCRAPE evaluation model) and Project CONDUIT (solving software transferability; $450,000 NSF grant; UT + Dartmouth, Iowa, Oregon State, North Carolina; strict pedagogical + technical review; a 1973 bilingual Mexico City workshop proving portability). Also details the CDC 6600's resistance to timesharing (Cray's "No, I don't think so" to a virtualization request; 6-bit characters, 17-bit memory limit, extended core swapping, PPUs hanging on novice input requiring nightly reboots).

PDP-10, DEC-10, DEC-20

The ~1975 acquisition of the HRC DEC-10 was the critical shift toward democratized, interactive computing (native 7-bit ASCII, virtual memory, interrupt-driven high-concurrency timesharing), decoupling interactive users from batch scientific loads and turning terminal rooms into "proto-online social worlds" (culminating in the 18-player DECWAR; an Australian recollection of seeing it in 1981). Extensive context on 1970s public computer fear (1971 AFIPS-Time survey: a third thought computers could "think"; HAL from 2001; Kemeny's warning about "computer illiterates"; teacher fear of replacement; student math anxiety) and UT's efforts (C-BE, OMNITAB, faculty workshops) to shift from "computational intimidation" to "interactive empowerment." The DEC-10 subverted the "Big Iron" image and the batch-processing "priesthood" (Ted Nelson's Computer Lib, 1974). Technical/marketing history of the PDP-10 architecture (1966, descendant of the PDP-6, competing with IBM's 7090; KA10/KI10/KL10/KS10 processors; MIT/Stanford AI research); rebranded DECsystem-10 (1971, TOPS-10) and DECSYSTEM-20 (1976, TOPS-20 from BBN's TENEX, paged virtual memory, command completion/help). Notes the counterculture-meets-military paradox (ITS at MIT with no passwords; WAITS at Stanford's bohemian SAIL; Stewart Brand's 1972 Rolling Stone piece, "the computer itself is a new LSD") — all ARPA/DARPA-funded.

New Frontiers

The UTCC's pioneering "frontier" spirit, embodied by director Charles Warlick ("Texans do not undertake things in a small way"; "There they go. I had better run and catch them, for I am their leader."). Recaps the Southwest Regional Educational Computer Network (grew to 23 institutions), the CONDUIT coalition, and 1977 (UT as the first ARPANET site in Texas). Details the 1973 "Dual Dinosaurs" (6600 + 6400, shared filesystem; 6400 running 128 timesharing ports, 6600 batch; ~18,000 undergraduates) — computing becoming an instructional utility.

RAND, SAGE, Timesharing

Timesharing on UT's 6600 was a student-led initiative by three grad students, notably Forest Baskett, who effectively ran the systems-programming staff. His inspiration: a 1964 summer job at RAND's spinoff System Development Corporation (SDC) — the world's first independent software company (from the SAGE project). There he used the AN/FSQ-32 (Q-32), a canceled SAGE Super Combat Center prototype that ARPA (under Licklider) repurposed for interactive-computing research ("Man-Computer Symbiosis"). Details the Q-32's architecture (PDP-1 front-end handling terminal I/O; quantum round-robin scheduler with full-image drum swapping; 30+ simultaneous users). Baskett taught himself Lisp and wrote an interpreter on it. The Q-32 also achieved the first transcontinental data exchange between two operating systems (linked to MIT Lincoln Lab's TX-2, October 1965) — a direct ARPANET precursor. Frustrated by the 6600's batch SCOPE OS (octal-second runtime limits, ~9-hour cap), Baskett's team got Jim Browne's backing ("Hmm, that could be fun. Let's try") and repurposed the 6600's PPUs to run timesharing. The initial RESPOND service started March 1967 (ran a decade), later replaced by TAURUS within UT-2D. The project prompted CDC and Lawrence Livermore to launch their own timesharing efforts. Baskett's later career: Demos OS for the Cray-1 at Los Alamos, VLSI research at Xerox PARC.

Southwest Network

Explores the deep parallel between timesharing and packet switching — both slice an expensive resource (CPU cycles / network bandwidth) to exploit the "bursty" nature of human-computer interaction, using multiplexing to create the illusion of dedicated access. Davies designed packet switching (1965) precisely because circuit-switched phone networks were incompatible with bursty timesharing traffic. The Q-32 was used for early networking (1963 300-mile link to SRI's CDC 160A, separating control and data lines). By 1969 this led to the NSF-funded Southwest Region Educational Computer Network (hub-and-spoke around the 6600/6400; 9 → 23 institutions; Southwest Texas State, Rice, Austin High, McCallum High, junior colleges). The network proved connectivity but exposed a content gap → the shift to educational software (Project C-BE, 1971; Allen, Lagowski, Culp). Highlights SIMPLE (Symbolic Interactive Matrix Processing Language) — a conversational matrix language and "direct ancestor of MATLAB," with a "Teach" command, used on Datapoint terminals. Quotes MATLAB creator Cleve Moler on the engineering-vs-CS divide (created MATLAB mid-70s at the University of New Mexico; UT/New Mexico connections via White Sands/Los Alamos). Also cites Mosmann's 1974 critique of the "network bandwagon" (installing lines ≠ a functional network; chronic under-utilization <5% off-campus), the mid-70s video-terminal transition, and all signs pointing toward the ARPANET arriving in 1977.

ARPANET And Internet

The Q-32 foreshadowed the 1977 ARPANET arrival. The 1965 Q-32/TX-2 experiment (Marill and Roberts; the "elementary approach"; a TX-2 user running a Lisp program on the Q-32 across the country) proved computers could talk to each other but exposed circuit-switching's fatal flaws (idle lines, bit-flip corruption, no error recovery), convincing Larry Roberts to adopt packet switching. Bob Taylor (ARPA IPTO director and UT Austin graduate) recruited Roberts. Wesley Clark's "You've got the network inside out" insight → the Interface Message Processor (IMP) decoupled architecture (BBN's ruggedized Honeywell DDP-516; the first network routers; 128-byte packets, address labels, routing tables). Application protocols: Telnet (RFC 15, 1969) and FTP (RFC 114, 1971; RFC 354, 1973; early email), built on the Network Control Program (1970). The 1972 "ARPANET Ball" (ICCC, Washington Hilton; Kahn; the PARRY/Doctor AI chat demo); the International Network Working Group (Cerf) → TCP/IP. UT's first IMP (1977, first in Texas) — but the HRC DEC-10 could not be the first host because stock TOPS-10 didn't support the IMP; instead a PDP-11/45 running hacked UNIX in the Daily Texan composing room became the UTEXAS host (long Clive Dawson quote). Later a PDP-11/70 in the Computation Center, then the DEC-20 in Painter Hall (UTEXAS-20); plus the Certifiable Minicomputer Project's thick encryption cable run down the Tower elevator shaft.

HRC And The DEC-10

The 1975 DEC-10 shifted campus culture toward interactive exploration, housed fittingly in the Harry Ransom Center (arts/humanities) near the Linguistics Research Center (a Clive Dawson quote about Dr. Helen Jo Hewitt / "HJ," a TECO power-user and "font hacker," using TECO macros to drive a daisy-wheel robotic typewriter for diacritics/Greek). Administrative appeal (compact, <$1M, <$20,000 site prep, reentrant compilers serving many users). Home to ICSCA (Don Good, Woody Bledsoe, Jim Browne; 20th/21st floors of the Tower) doing program verification — the Gypsy Verification Environment and the Certifiable Minicomputer Project (late 70s), which mathematically verified ARPANET security code replicating BBN's Private Line Interface (PLI, edge cryptography / selective payload encryption, ancestor of IPsec/HAIPE; NSA-approved 1975); the UT team verified a ~5,000-line Gypsy cryptographic gateway interoperating with BBN hardware. Also covers DECUS software-sharing tapes, the community fostered by Bboard/GRIPE utilities, the close-knit staff, and eventual obsolescence (32-bit VAX). The DEC-10 was decommissioned October 31, 1982 (Dawson's "The Soul of an Old Machine").

Pioneers

Situates UT's 70s computing in the national hacker/community-computing milieu (Homebrew Computer Club at SLAC; Stanford/MIT AI Labs; ARPANET's SF-LOVERS mailing list; Ray Tomlinson's 1971 email; ARPA's "conscious leniency" toward social lists/games as a talent-retention subsidy). Detailed lineage of the Star Trek game: Mike Mayfield's 1971 text version on a UCLA SDS Sigma 7 (which was also the very first ARPANET computer) → 1972 HP 2000C BASIC rewrite (STTR1) → Dave Ahl and Mary Cole's 1973 DEC BASIC port (SPACWR), published in Ahl's 101 BASIC Computer Games (first million-selling computer book). A separate UT branch: Grady Hicks and Jim Korp's 1973 BASIC variant on the 6600 (infamous for printing slow Marcus Aurelius quotes at 110 baud) → Matuszek and Reynolds's 1973–74 Fortran rewrite (stars going nova, "The Thing") → a two-player "WAR" (~1976). Ahl's magazine Creative Computing re-entered with a 1976 article "Computing At The University of Texas" (photo of the DEC-10 with staff Pat Caroom, Judith West, Elissa Vogel) — unwittingly covering the machine on which the 1978 "ultimate version" (DECWAR) would be created. Notes the DEC-10's 36-bit precision (single ~8 digits, double ~18 digits) and the arrival of green-phosphor video terminals for CS grad students by 1974 (Dave Matuszek in Pearce Hall).

Teletypes And Cathode Ray Tubes

Campus geography of computing ca. 1970–75: Pearce Hall (Old Law Building) Room 105 RJE; teletypes locked in the W.C. Hogg Building; CS in Waggener Hall (1971) then Painter Hall (1972, shared with Physics, "Home of Star Trek"); Taylor Hall Annex RJE (torn down for the ACES building); the MCC building "stealing" CS's planned building slot. Pearce Hall as "temporary institutional repurposing" (obsolete buildings used for terminal rooms). The mixed teletype/video-terminal era, guided by the Faculty Computer Committee (Jim Browne, 20 years). Long history of San Antonio's Datapoint (Computer Terminal Corporation, founded 1968 by Phil Ray — UT '57 — and Gus Roche; Bob McClure's advice to build a "glass teletype" emulating the Teletype Model 33): the Datapoint 3300 (1969, replacing the loud ASR-33; casings outsourced to a motorcycle-helmet maker; rebadged as DEC VT06, HP 2600A) and the Datapoint 2200 (1970, "true birth of the personal computer"; instruction set → Intel 8008 → x86; little-endian legacy; punchcard-shaped "squashed" screen; dual cassette drives; the Pillsbury plant running standalone). Traces the terminal-to-PC evolution and the 1978 DEC VT100 (Intel 8080 CPU, ANSI X3.64 escape sequences, on-screen setup, smooth scrolling, 19,200 baud). Constrained reality remained: 300/1200-baud dial-in, greenbar fanfold listings.

Simulation And AI

Contrasts two worldviews. The classic assembly + Fortran symbiosis (inner loops in assembly, outer/one-time code in Fortran) defined the numerical-simulation era; DECWAR was among the last projects in this tradition, while contemporaneous UTOPIA was nearly pure Fortran (assembly hidden in portable libraries) — both effectively large simulations (a satellite in a gravity field vs. 18 people battling across a galaxy). By the 70s a different AI spirit took root (human language, real-world reasoning). Detailed PDP-10 environment ca. 1975 (36-bit word-addressable; 18-bit halfwords/addressing; paging; ASCII/SIXBIT packing; first 16 words as fast registers used as an instruction cache in early Lisp). MACRO-10 (two-pass assembler, UUOs — unimplemented user operations as software instructions/system calls). FORTRAN-10 (advanced optimizer rivaling assembly; shared upper-segment memory with locking). The Certifiable Minicomputer Project (Don Good, 1975; Gypsy, a Pascal-derived language+specification environment; tools in Lisp — SID, VCG, theorem prover); the 1977 Encrypted Packet Interface (4,200–5,000 lines of Gypsy mechanically proven to duplicate BBN's black box); the Message Flow Modulator (first mechanically-proven software deployed in military security, passing all tests on the first attempt). Lisp projects at the Linguistics Research Center (founded 1961 by Winfred Lehmann; early Fortran German-English machine translation on the 6600; the 1966 ALPAC report collapse; Siemens's 1978 revival of METAL, rebuilt in Lisp on the DEC-10 by Jonathan Slocum, 1979, delivered 1984). Also Lauri Karttunen's KIMMO parser, Frances Karttunen's Nahuatl/Maya work, and the Cognitive Science program under Robert Simmons (from SDC — another RAND/SAGE/Q-32 link; Synthex/Protosynthex; the Q-32's Lisp 1.5 compiler-first port and the failed, memory-exhausting Lisp 2, canceled 1967).

TECO-124, MACRO-10, FORTRAN-10, DECWAR

The climactic section, first finishing the Lisp story: UT-LISP (native Lisp 1.5 in CDC COMPASS assembly on the 6600, built for reliability vs. flaky remote SDC connections) with its unique three-pointer cons cell (CAR/CDR/CSR partitioning the 60-bit word), ideal for semantic-network triples; Mabry Tyson's virtual memory; migrating Protosynthex and rewriting METAL; and LAWALY (Siklóssy and Dreussi's UT-LISP robot planner, a "robot-janitor" across 20+ simulated worlds, benchmarked favorably against SRI's STRIPS). Then DECWAR's full lineage: BASIC (Hicks/Korp 1973) → Fortran single-player (Matuszek, Reynolds, Cohen 1973–74) → two-player "WAR" (Schneider et al.) → DECWAR on the DEC-10 (Hysick, Potter; guidance from Clive Dawson, Tommy Loomis, Rick Watson; name honoring the CDC WAR and MIT's 1962 Spacewar). The DEC-10's shared high-segment memory + inter-process locking enabled up to 18 players (each an independent job) sharing one "game board" in core memory. Deep technical detail:

  • A custom TECO toolchain auto-generated Fortran include files (HISEG.FOR, LOWSEG.FOR, EXTERN.FOR from MSG.MAC) to keep Fortran symbols aligned with assembly memory offsets. History of TECO (Dan Murphy, 1962, PDP-1; "Tape/Text Editor and Corrector"; pointer "dot"; YAFIYGI; evolution into Emacs, 1976, then GNU Emacs 1984); UT's TECO-124 (Dawson, with video-terminal display logic, vs. DEC's teletype-era TECO-24).
  • MACRO-10 as a highly programmable macro processor (searching the macro table before the op-code table, so macros can override hardware instructions); DEFINE syntax, default args, unique labels (%), concatenation ('), string evaluation; nesting to 18 levels; integration with the DDT symbolic debugger for interactive, high-level-feeling workflows (Gates & Allen used MACRO-10 + DDT on a Harvard PDP-10 to write an 8080 emulator for Altair BASIC, ~1975). Described as democratized and approachable (Singer's 1978 and Gorin's 1985 intro books; a Singer quote).
  • FORTRAN-10 meeting assembly halfway: Backus's 1954 "automatic programming"; the 704 hardware shaping Fortran syntax; Cray's "I want a computer that runs Fortran"; the FORTRAN-10 global optimizer (up to 40% faster code); static memory allocation (no recursion → aggressive optimization); COMMON/EQUIVALENCE for low-level memory control and type-punning; subroutine linkage conventions as early ABIs; the eventual fade of hand-coded assembly into standardized libraries; and pre-Fortran-77 text handling as bit-masking of Hollerith constants (still six 6-bit uppercase chars per word — directly shaping DECWAR's design).
  • DECWAR's game mechanics as "classic mainframe elements": each player = a TOPS-10 job; turn-based at core (nothing happens unless a player acts, like play-by-mail); the "game board" = a shared high-segment core-memory chunk under lock. The Romulan (evolved from "The Thing") had no job of its own — its behavior emerged cooperatively from player jobs; it "spoke" via radio messages, convincing 80s players it was a real malevolent person; pathing bugs (steering into black holes; the Raven→Manta rename to avoid parser collision with "R"). Dual dataflows (attack + radio message linked lists in static core regions, with a boundary-overrun bug); message handling required MACRO-10 UUOs to lock/unlock shared memory — the root reason pure Fortran was infeasible and the code became bound to TOPS-10 (unportable even to TOPS-20/TENEX with its JSYS calls and PA1050 emulator's limits).
  • Survival and preservation: DEC canceled the PDP-10 line (1983), DEC itself died (1998), but DECWAR survives via Obsolescence Guaranteed (the PiDP-10 replica running SIMH on a Raspberry Pi) and Docker time capsules (SIMH + TOPS-10 + the reconstructed UT Source Distribution Tape), plus the ARPANET Reconstruction Project (Docker Compose orchestrating HRC DEC-10, Painter Hall DEC-20, and IMP containers with Telnet/FTP links). Anyone can now boot TOPS-10 and type r gam:decwar, and edit the code in original TECO/MACRO-10/FORTRAN-10.

Conclusion

Argues for preserving the 1958–1982 mainframe-era history of modeling and simulation in Austin and Houston through the code and the people, tracing the thread from Los Alamos human computers → Santa Monica/Houston → Austin, via Simplex, ADI, SOR, subsurface, and orbit determination (and possibly back to mechanical/analog models). These developments were mathematical at their core — so even without original 1953 source code, the machines (e.g., the IBM CPC) and exact mathematical methods are known, and the models can be faithfully reconstructed and run (the assembly/Fortran being effectively the same either way). Proposes Docker "time capsules" — self-contained, version-controlled, automated environments (hardware emulation + OS + tools + code + docs), with AI as an enabling partner. Beyond archival use, these could serve working modelers, aspiring to be "a kind of Feynman Lectures of modeling" (invoking Feynman's first-principles, minimalist clarity). The proposed "heartbeat" health check for a time capsule is Feynman's Lectures on Physics Table 22-3 (from the Algebra lecture), which produces continuous oscillation from pure arithmetic (exponents and imaginary numbers) — implementable in a few lines of assembly or Fortran as a "sign of life."

High Frontier Computing
Home

Austin & Houston, Texas

High Frontier Computing 1958 to 1982 — a history of numerical modeling and simulation in the mainframe era.
